_provenance.source_pdf: Goodrick, Mick - Almanac of Guitar Voice Leading, Vol 3.pdf

usage_notes.narrative: Goodrick places triads in the M-Lode as 3-part structures whose interval content consists primarily of 3rds and 6ths with some 4ths and 5ths, but containing no 2nds or 7ths. This interval profile distinguishes them categorically from 3-part 4th voicings. Chapter 4, p. 8.

Interval omission is permitted within the triad family — Goodrick states that 'the omission of interval types only occurs within particular 3-part chord families (triad; 3-part 4th; spread cluster).' Chapter 4, p. 8.

Goodrick teaches that dropping one voice from a 4-part 7th chord produces two possible triadic 3-part types: the 7th chord without its 3rd, or the 7th chord without its 5th. Each resulting 3-part triad type appears across four different 4-part chord families, creating a symmetry the student should exploit for reharmonization. Chapter 5, p. 9.

Goodrick recommends 3-part chords — including triads — over 4-part chords for guitarists: '3-part chords are easier to play than 4-part chords. Also, they often afford more space between the voices for melodic embellishment.' Chapter 11, p. 71.

All twenty foundational 3-part chord types in Chapter 11 — including triads — are derived from three source scales: Major, Melodic Minor, and Harmonic Minor, transposed to the root of C. The student must then transpose to remaining keys independently. Chapter 11, p. 71.

For triads moving through a diatonic scale, Goodrick identifies that Volumes I and II used only three of six possible generic voice-leading patterns. Volume III introduces the remaining alternates; the student should apply all six A-B-C generic patterns to triads. Chapter 10, p. 56.

To learn all inversions of a chord type, Goodrick prescribes the Grip-Slipping technique: cycle through inversions using Drop 3 voicings within a whole-tone (six-tonic) system. May also try Drop 2 and Drop 2&4. This is Specific Chromatic Voice-Leading (SCVL). Chapter 12, p. 161.
Goodrick prescribes splitting 4-part voicings into two-voice duets — top two voices and bottom two voices — and adding passing tones. He notes this is 'NICE in Harmonic minor!' Chapter 10, p. 43.

Because each 3-part chord type appears inside exactly four different 4-part chord families, Goodrick teaches the student to substitute any of the four parent families when harmonizing a given 3-part sonority. Chapter 5, p. 9.

Goodrick classifies stacked-fourth chords (both 3-part and 4-part) as sus4 structures within the M-Lode. He recommends naming them sus4: 'My suggestion for a suitable name for this chord would be: G [sus4]. That means a G Major triad with 4 suspended for 3.' Chapter 2, p. 4.

Goodrick prescribes sus4 notation as the preferred label for all stacked-fourth chords, rejecting more cumbersome alternatives. For 4-part 4ths: 'Sus 4 Chords... I think it's the best way to go.' Chapter 2, pp. 4-5.

3-part 4th voicings (sus4 structures) belong to the family class in which interval omission is permitted, alongside triads and spread clusters. The student may omit interval types within 3-part 4th voicings without leaving the family. Chapter 4, p. 8.
Goodrick defines 3-part 4th voicings as primarily consisting of 4ths and 5ths with some 2nds and 7ths, but containing no 3rds or 6ths — the inverse of the triad's interval profile. Chapter 4, p. 8.

Goodrick uses CMaj7 as the primary worked example for deriving 3-part chords from a 4-part 7th chord, positioning it as structure number 1 in the 35-structure taxonomy. Dropping the 3rd yields a 7th-no-3rd voicing; dropping the 5th yields a 7th-no-5th voicing. Chapter 5, p. 9.

For CMaj7-type 4-part chords, Goodrick teaches the full menu of voicing transformations: 4-way close, Drop 2, Drop 3, Drop 2&3, Drop 2&4, and Double Drop 2 Drop 3, applied across root position, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd inversions. Chapter 5, p. 9; Chapter 11.
